Module 3 · O. Levenspiel Ch. 18 to §18.3 · H. S. Fogler Ch. 15 to §15.3.1

Pore diffusion, Thiele modulus and the effectiveness factor

When reactant must diffuse into a porous pellet, the inside sees a lower concentration than the outside. The effectiveness factor measures the loss; the Thiele modulus predicts it.

OL 18 intro, 18.1, 18.2, 18.3HSF 15.1, 15.2, 15.3.1Lectures 1–11 Sep 2026
Exam focus, from the professor

Know: how to formulate the problem (balance, flux, rate law, boundary conditions, dimensionless form), what η\etaη and the Thiele modulus mean, and how to use them. Not the focus: solving the differential equation. Solutions are included below, marked "for understanding", so the η\etaη formulas are not a mystery.

1The spectrum of kinetic regimes (Levenspiel, Ch. 18 introduction)

Catalysts can speed a reaction a million-fold, but for mixtures such as petroleum the most important property is selectivity. Some general observations (OL): catalyst selection is still largely trial and error; copying a good catalyst's chemical composition does not guarantee activity (physical structure matters; heating above a critical temperature can destroy activity); a catalyst lowers the energy barrier but never changes the equilibrium; a large accessible surface is needed.

For a porous catalyst particle bathed by reactant A, the rate for the particle as a whole may depend on five factors:

Factor (OL Table 18.1)Porous catalyst particleCatalyst-coated surfaceBurning fuel dropletCells, simple creatures
1 Surface reactionYesYesNoYes
2 Pore diffusionYesNoNoMaybe
3 Particle ΔT\Delta TΔTNot too likelyNoNoNo
4 Film ΔT\Delta TΔTSometimesRareAll importantNo
5 Film mass transferNoYesAll importantCould be

2§18.1 The rate equation for surface kinetics

The active-site theory views three successive steps at the surface: (1) a molecule adsorbs on an active site; (2) it reacts with a molecule on an adjacent site (dual site), with one from the gas (single site), or simply decomposes (single site); (3) products desorb and free the site. All species are assumed to be in equilibrium except in the controlling step. Every such rate law has the form

OL 18.1rate of reaction=(kinetic term)(driving force or displacement from equilibrium)(resistance term)\text{rate of reaction} = \frac{(\text{kinetic term})(\text{driving force or displacement from equilibrium})}{(\text{resistance term})}rate of reaction=(resistance term)(kinetic term)(driving force or displacement from equilibrium)​

For A+B⇌R+SA + B \rightleftharpoons R + SA+B⇌R+S with an inert carrier U present:

adsorption of A controls:−rA′′=k (pA−pRpS/KpB)(1+KApRpS/KpB+KBpB+KRpR+KSpS+KUpU)2\text{adsorption of A controls:}\quad -r''_A = \frac{k\,(p_A - p_Rp_S/Kp_B)}{\left(1 + K_Ap_Rp_S/Kp_B + K_Bp_B + K_Rp_R + K_Sp_S + K_Up_U\right)^2}adsorption of A controls:−rA′′​=(1+KA​pR​pS​/KpB​+KB​pB​+KR​pR​+KS​pS​+KU​pU​)2k(pA​−pR​pS​/KpB​)​
surface reaction between adjacent adsorbed A and B controls:−rA′′=k (pApB−pRpS/K)(1+KApA+KBpB+KRpR+KSpS+KUpU)2\text{surface reaction between adjacent adsorbed A and B controls:}\quad -r''_A = \frac{k\,(p_Ap_B - p_Rp_S/K)}{\left(1 + K_Ap_A + K_Bp_B + K_Rp_R + K_Sp_S + K_Up_U\right)^2}surface reaction between adjacent adsorbed A and B controls:−rA′′​=(1+KA​pA​+KB​pB​+KR​pR​+KS​pS​+KU​pU​)2k(pA​pB​−pR​pS​/K)​

These carry three to seven adjustable constants. Levenspiel then argues not to use them for design:

For: truth and predictability

If the true mechanism is found, extrapolation to new conditions is much safer.

Against: finding the mechanism

With 3–7 constants per model, you must show one family fits so much better that all others are rejected. Differences are usually within experimental error (Chou's analysis of 18 mechanisms for the codimer example). A good fit is only "one of good fit", not reality.

Against: combining resistances

Combining a multi-constant surface rate with pore or film diffusion becomes impractical. Replace it by an equivalent first-order expression.

Summary on surface kinetics

Most catalytic conversion data can be fitted adequately by simple first- or nth-order rate expressions (Prater and Lago). So use the simplest correlating expression, first- or nth-order kinetics, for the surface reaction. This also matches Fogler §10.3.7: at high temperature the Langmuir–Hinshelwood denominator tends to 1.

Small mLmLmL (mL<0.4mL < 0.4mL<0.4)

η≈1\eta\approx1η≈1. Concentration barely drops; pore diffusion offers negligible resistance. A small mLmLmL means a short pore, slow reaction or rapid diffusion.

Large mLmLmL (mL>4mL > 4mL>4)

η≈1/mL\eta\approx1/mLη≈1/mL. Concentration drops to zero close to the mouth. Strong pore resistance: diffusion strongly influences the rate.

Volume change on reaction (OL Fig. 18.5)

If the reaction expands the gas (εA>0\varepsilon_A>0εA​>0), extra outflow from the pore makes it harder for reactant to diffuse in, lowering η\etaη. Contraction pulls fluid in and raises η\etaη. For first order, Thiele found this simply shifts the η\etaη vs MTM_TMT​ curve.

5§18.3 Porous catalyst particles

The single-pore result approximates particles of any shape once three things are replaced:

  1. Diffusion coefficient. Replace the molecular diffusivity D\mathscr{D}D by the effective diffusivity De\mathscr{D}_eDe​ in the porous structure (values in Weisz 1959; see §7 below for Fogler's estimate).
  2. Particle size. Use the characteristic length L=(volume of particleexterior surface available for reactant penetration)={thickness2flat plate (both faces)R2cylinderR3sphereL = \left(\frac{\text{volume of particle}}{\text{exterior surface available for reactant penetration}}\right) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\text{thickness}}{2} & \text{flat plate (both faces)}\\[2mm] \dfrac{R}{2} & \text{cylinder}\\[2mm] \dfrac{R}{3} & \text{sphere}\end{cases}L=(exterior surface available for reactant penetrationvolume of particle​)=⎩⎨⎧​2thickness​2R​3R​​flat plate (both faces)cylindersphere​
  3. Rate measure. Use −rA′′′=k′′′CA-r'''_A = k'''C_A−rA′′′​=k′′′CA​ per volume of particle.

MTM_TMT​ needs k′′′k'''k′′′, which is what you are trying to measure. The trick is a modulus built only from observable quantities. Since −rA,obs′′′=η k′′′CAs-r'''_{A,obs} = \eta\,k'''C_{As}−rA,obs′′′​=ηk′′′CAs​:

OL 25diffusion-free:rA1′rA2′=η1k′CAη2k′CA=η1η2=1strong resistance:rA1′rA2′=η1η2=MT2MT1=R2R1\text{diffusion-free:}\quad \frac{r'_{A1}}{r'_{A2}} = \frac{\eta_1k'C_A}{\eta_2k'C_A} = \frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2} = 1\qquad\qquad \text{strong resistance:}\quad \frac{r'_{A1}}{r'_{A2}} = \frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2} = \frac{M_{T2}}{M_{T1}} = \frac{R_2}{R_1}diffusion-free:rA2′​rA1′​​=η2​k′CA​η1​k′CA​​=η2​η1​​=1strong resistance:rA2′​rA1′​​=η2​η1​​=MT1​MT2​​=R1​R2​​

In the strong-resistance regime the rate varies inversely with particle size. This is the standard experimental test: crush the catalyst; if the rate per mass does not change, there is no pore resistance.

Levenspiel closes §18.3 by collecting the first-order results in one place:

OL 34−rA′′′=k′′′CAs E,E=tanh⁡MTMT,MT=Lk′′′De,MW=MT2 E=L2 (−rA,obs′′′)CA,obs De-r'''_A = k'''C_{As}\,\mathscr{E},\qquad \mathscr{E} = \frac{\tanh M_T}{M_T},\qquad M_T = L\sqrt{\frac{k'''}{\mathscr{D}_e}},\qquad M_W = M_T^2\,\mathscr{E} = \frac{L^2\,(-r'''_{A,obs})}{C_{A,obs}\,\mathscr{D}_e}−rA′′′​=k′′′CAs​E,E=MT​tanhMT​​,MT​=LDe​k′′′​​,MW​=MT2​E=CA,obs​De​L2(−rA,obs′′′​)​

k′′′CAsk'''C_{As}k′′′CAs​

The rate without any diffusion effects. E=1\mathscr{E} = 1E=1 means no diffusion resistance.

E\mathscr{E}E, effectiveness factor

A "fudge factor" between 0 and 1 that accounts for the resistance to pore diffusion. The flat-plate expression tanh⁡MT/MT\tanh M_T/M_TtanhMT​/MT​ is a good approximation for all particle shapes.

LLL and De\mathscr{D}_eDe​

LLL: characteristic length (particle volume over external area). De\mathscr{D}_eDe​: effective diffusion coefficient in the porous solid, m3 gas/(m solid⋅s)\mathrm{m^3\ gas/(m\ solid\cdot s)}m3 gas/(m solid⋅s).

MTM_TMT​, Thiele modulus

Useful for predicting reactor behaviour from known kinetic information, that is, a known k′′′k'''k′′′.

MWM_WMW​, Weisz modulus

Useful for interpreting experiments, since it contains only observables.

How to use them

Evaluate MTM_TMT​ or MWM_WMW​, find E\mathscr{E}E from the equations or figures, and put E\mathscr{E}E into the rate equation.

Desirable processing range (OL eq. 35)

Fine solids are free of pore-diffusion resistance but are difficult to use: imagine the pressure drop of a packed bed of face powder. A bed of large particles has a small Δp\Delta pΔp but is liable to be in the regime of strong pore diffusion, where much of each pellet's interior is unused. For the most effective operation, use the largest particle size that is still free of diffusional resistance:

MT≅0.4orMW≅0.15M_T \cong 0.4\qquad\text{or}\qquad M_W \cong 0.15MT​≅0.4orMW​≅0.15

6Extensions (OL §18.3)

Mixture of particle shapes and sizes (Aris)

ηˉ=η1f1′+η2f2′+⋯\bar\eta = \eta_1f'_1 + \eta_2f'_2 + \cdotsηˉ​=η1​f1′​+η2​f2′​+⋯

fi′f'_ifi′​ = volume fraction of particles of size/shape iii in the bed.

Molar volume change

Why this matters

If you measure kinetics on large pellets without checking for pore resistance, you will report the wrong order and roughly half the true activation energy, and your design will fail when pellet size or temperature changes. Fogler calls this falsified kinetics (§15.4, just beyond the syllabus limit).

7Effective diffusivity (HSF 15.1, 15.2.1)

Homogeneous systems first (15.1). One-dimensional steady diffusion with reaction, dilute, through a stagnant film:

−dWAzdz+rA=0,WAz=−DABdCAdz⇒DABd2CAdz2+rA=0-\frac{dW_{Az}}{dz} + r_A = 0,\qquad W_{Az} = -D_{AB}\frac{dC_A}{dz}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad D_{AB}\frac{d^2C_A}{dz^2} + r_A = 0−dzdWAz​​+rA​=0,WAz​=−DAB​dzdCA​​⇒DAB​dz2d2CA​​+rA​=0

In a pellet, pores are not straight cylinders but tortuous, interconnected paths of pore bodies and throats. Rather than model each path, define an effective diffusivity that describes the average diffusion at a radial position, with the flux based on the total area (voids and solids) normal to transport, 4πr24\pi r^24πr2.

15-1De=DAB φp σcτ~D_e = \frac{D_{AB}\,\varphi_p\,\sigma_c}{\tilde\tau}De​=τ~DAB​φp​σc​​

φp\varphi_pφp​ pellet porosity

φp=volume of void spacetotal volume (voids + solids)\varphi_p = \frac{\text{volume of void space}}{\text{total volume (voids + solids)}}φp​=total volume (voids + solids)volume of void space​

Not all of the area normal to the flux is open.

τ~\tilde\tauτ~ tortuosity

τ~=actual distance travelled between two pointsshortest distance between them\tilde\tau = \frac{\text{actual distance travelled between two points}}{\text{shortest distance between them}}τ~=shortest distance between themactual distance travelled between two points​

Paths are tortuous. Typical 3; values of 6–10 are common.

σc\sigma_cσc​ constriction factor

Pores vary in cross-section. Depends on the ratio of maximum to minimum pore area: 1 when A1=A2A_1 = A_2A1​=A2​, about 0.5 when A1/A2=10A_1/A_2 = 10A1​/A2​=10. Some authors lump τ~/σc\tilde\tau/\sigma_cτ~/σc​ into one "tortuosity factor".

How to reduce internal diffusion limitation

Lower ϕ\phiϕ: use smaller pellets (smaller RRR), raise DeD_eDe​ (larger pores, higher porosity, lower tortuosity), or put the active metal only in an outer shell. Raising temperature makes it worse (kkk grows faster than DeD_eDe​).

11Self-test

Define the effectiveness factor and the Thiele modulus in words.

η\etaη: actual overall rate in the pellet divided by the rate if the whole interior were at the external surface concentration and temperature. Thiele modulus: square root of the ratio of a characteristic surface reaction rate to a characteristic diffusion rate; it tells how far reactant penetrates before it reacts.

A reaction in 1 mm particles gives the same rate per gram as in 0.2 mm particles. Conclusion?

Rate independent of size: diffusion-free regime, η≈1\eta \approx 1η≈1 for both. The measured rate is the intrinsic rate. (If it had fallen five-fold, strong pore resistance.)

True order 2, Etrue=150E_{true} = 150Etrue​=150 kJ/mol. What order and activation energy would you observe on large pellets at high temperature?

Order (2+1)/2=1.5(2+1)/2 = 1.5(2+1)/2=1.5. Eobs=(Etrue+Ediff)/2≈(150+5 to 15)/2≈78E_{obs} = (E_{true}+E_{diff})/2 \approx (150 + 5\text{ to }15)/2 \approx 78Eobs​=(Etrue​+Ediff​)/2≈(150+5 to 15)/2≈78–838383 kJ/mol, roughly 75 kJ/mol if EdiffE_{diff}Ediff​ is neglected.

Why is MWM_WMW​ useful when MTM_TMT​ already exists?

MTM_TMT​ contains the intrinsic k′′′k'''k′′′, unknown if the measurement was already slowed by diffusion. MW=L2(−rA′′′)obs/(DeCAs)M_W = L^2(-r'''_A)_{obs}/(\mathscr{D}_eC_{As})MW​=L2(−rA′′′​)obs​/(De​CAs​) uses only the observed rate, measured size, surface concentration and effective diffusivity, so it diagnoses the regime directly.

Why does the flux in the spherical shell balance use 4πr24\pi r^24πr2 (total area) and not the pore area?

Because DeD_eDe​ is defined to include the porosity (and tortuosity, constriction): De=DABφpσc/τ~D_e = D_{AB}\varphi_p\sigma_c/\tilde\tauDe​=DAB​φp​σc​/τ~. The flux WAr=−De dCA/drW_{Ar} = -D_e\,dC_A/drWAr​=−De​dCA​/dr is then per unit total area.

Levenspiel recommends a "desirable processing range" for particle size. What is it, and why?

Use the largest particles that are still free of pore-diffusion resistance: MT≅0.4M_T \cong 0.4MT​≅0.4 or MW≅0.15M_W \cong 0.15MW​≅0.15 (OL eq. 35). Smaller particles use their whole interior but give a very large bed pressure drop; larger ones have a small Δp\Delta pΔp but leave much of each pellet's interior unused.

Under strong internal diffusion limitation, how does the rate depend on pellet diameter and on gas velocity?

−rA=3RDek1 CAs-r_A = \dfrac{3}{R}\sqrt{D_ek_1}\,C_{As}−rA​=R3​De​k1​​CAs​ (Fogler 15-34 with 15-33): inversely proportional to pellet size. Gas velocity has a negligible effect, because the limitation is inside the pellet, not in the external film.
